questions.stem: This figure traces fluid moving out of the capillary into the interstitium and perivascular space, then into the alveoli. What condition is being illustrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Emphysema

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pleural effusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary embolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pneumothorax

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary edema

explanation.summary: Fluid leaving the capillary first accumulates in the interstitium/perivascular space and then floods the alveoli, the sequence of pulmonary edema formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluid leaving the capillary first accumulates in the interstitium/perivascular space and then floods the alveoli, the sequence of pulmonary edema formation.

questions.stem: As pulmonary arterial pressure or cardiac output rises, the two capillary changes shown here occur. What is their net effect on pulmonary vascular resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reduces total pulmonary blood flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has no effect on pulmonary vascular resistance

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases pulmonary vascular resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: It decreases pulmonary vascular resistance

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases alveolar dead space

explanation.summary: Recruitment of previously closed capillaries and distension of already-open ones lower pulmonary vascular resistance as flow and pressure rise, keeping pulmonary pressures low.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recruitment of previously closed capillaries and distension of already-open ones lower pulmonary vascular resistance as flow and pressure rise, keeping pulmonary pressures low.

questions.stem: This U-shaped curve relates pulmonary vascular resistance to lung volume, with a minimum at functional residual capacity. Why does resistance rise again at total lung capacity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surfactant is depleted at total lung capacity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alveolar capillaries are stretched and compressed by the expanded alveoli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blood viscosity increases at high lung volumes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypoxic vasoconstriction is maximal at high lung volumes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extra-alveolar vessels collapse from loss of radial traction

explanation.summary: PVR is lowest near FRC. At high volumes the alveolar capillaries are stretched and squeezed by distended alveoli; at low volumes extra-alveolar vessels narrow from lost radial traction, so PVR rises at both extremes.
explanation.whyCorrect: PVR is lowest near FRC. At high volumes the alveolar capillaries are stretched and squeezed by distended alveoli; at low volumes extra-alveolar vessels narrow from lost radial traction, so PVR rises at both extremes.

questions.stem: In this figure an alveolus with low oxygen triggers narrowing of its supplying pulmonary artery while a normal alveolus keeps its vessel open. What is the physiological benefit of this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases anatomic dead space ventilation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It diverts blood from poorly ventilated toward better ventilated alveoli

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases blood flow to hypoxic regions to raise oxygen uptake

choices.label: D
choices.text: It dilates capillaries to prevent pulmonary edema

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lowers systemic arterial blood pressure

explanation.summary: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction shunts blood away from hypoxic alveoli toward well-oxygenated regions, optimizing ventilation-perfusion matching.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction shunts blood away from hypoxic alveoli toward well-oxygenated regions, optimizing ventilation-perfusion matching.

questions.stem: This graph shows pulmonary blood flow falling steeply as alveolar PO2 drops below roughly 100 mmHg. Which mechanism produces this relationship?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon dioxide-mediated bronchodilation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Systemic baroreceptor reflex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bohr effect on hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Laplace-driven alveolar collapse

explanation.summary: Low alveolar PO2 constricts local pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to poorly oxygenated regions of the lung.
explanation.whyCorrect: Low alveolar PO2 constricts local pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to poorly oxygenated regions of the lung.

questions.stem: This diagram shows the pressures acting across the alveolar-capillary interface, plus lymphatic drainage. What outcome do these balanced forces normally prevent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffusion of oxygen into the capillary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accumulation of fluid in the alveoli

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronchoconstriction of the small airways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of the capillary endothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Collapse of the alveolus during expiration

explanation.summary: Capillary hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures, interstitial forces, and lymphatic drainage normally balance so the alveoli stay dry; disrupting this balance causes pulmonary edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capillary hydrostatic and colloid osmotic pressures, interstitial forces, and lymphatic drainage normally balance so the alveoli stay dry; disrupting this balance causes pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: This figure divides the upright lung into regions where blood flows 'with gravity' versus 'against gravity.' What does it illustrate about pulmonary perfusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gravity has no effect on pulmonary blood flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blood flow is greater at the apex than at the base

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ventilation exceeds perfusion at the base

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood flow is greater at the lung base than at the apex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perfusion is uniform throughout the upright lung

explanation.summary: In the upright lung, gravity increases perfusion toward the base and reduces it at the apex, producing a vertical gradient of blood flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the upright lung, gravity increases perfusion toward the base and reduces it at the apex, producing a vertical gradient of blood flow.

questions.stem: This figure divides the upright lung into three regions defined by the relationships among alveolar, arterial, and venous pressures. In the uppermost region, alveolar pressure exceeds arterial pressure. What happens to blood flow there?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flow reverses back toward the pulmonary artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flow is maximal because the vessels are fully distended

choices.label: C
choices.text: Flow is driven by lymphatic drainage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flow ceases because alveolar pressure collapses the capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Flow depends only on the arterial-to-venous pressure difference

explanation.summary: In West Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial > venous pressure), alveolar pressure compresses the capillaries and no flow occurs; this zone is normally absent in healthy people.
explanation.whyCorrect: In West Zone 1 (alveolar > arterial > venous pressure), alveolar pressure compresses the capillaries and no flow occurs; this zone is normally absent in healthy people.

questions.stem: This curve plots hemoglobin O2 saturation against PO2. What best explains its characteristic S (sigmoidal) shape?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Denaturation of hemoglobin at high oxygen tensions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competitive inhibition of O2 binding by dissolved CO2 in plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Saturating first-order kinetics of a single independent binding site

choices.label: D
choices.text: A linear one-to-one relationship between dissolved plasma O2 and saturation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cooperative binding

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin's four subunits bind O2 cooperatively, so affinity rises as successive sites are occupied, producing the sigmoid curve that steepens over the physiological range and plateaus near full saturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin's four subunits bind O2 cooperatively, so affinity rises as successive sites are occupied, producing the sigmoid curve that steepens over the physiological range and plateaus near full saturation.

questions.stem: In the lungs, hemoglobin binds O2 while releasing CO2 and H+; in the tissues it does the reverse. Which principle does this reciprocal exchange illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H+ binding permanently oxidizes heme iron to methemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of CO2/H+ lowers hemoglobin's O2 affinity, and O2 binding lowers its affinity for CO2/H+

choices.label: C
choices.text: O2 and CO2 compete for the same heme iron binding site

choices.label: D
choices.text: CO2 is carried exclusively bound to the heme groups

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemoglobin transports all CO2 as carbaminohemoglobin only

explanation.summary: In tissues, high CO2 and H+ promote O2 release (Bohr effect); in lungs, O2 loading drives off CO2 and H+ (Haldane effect). These allosteric shifts optimize gas exchange at each site.
explanation.whyCorrect: In tissues, high CO2 and H+ promote O2 release (Bohr effect); in lungs, O2 loading drives off CO2 and H+ (Haldane effect). These allosteric shifts optimize gas exchange at each site.

questions.imageRef: repic-798_Brick Exchange - Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Transport_p14_1.png

questions.stem: This diagram traces CO2 handling in a red blood cell at the tissues and again at the lungs. What is the role of the enzyme shown catalyzing the reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It splits hemoglobin to release stored oxygen

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds CO2 directly to form carbaminohemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: It actively pumps chloride out of the red cell against its gradient

choices.label: D
choices.text: It buffers plasma pH by consuming free bicarbonate

choices.label: E
choices.text: It rapidly interconverts CO2 and water with carbonic acid

explanation.summary: Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O to H2CO3, which dissociates to HCO3- and H+. Bicarbonate exits the cell (chloride shift) so ~70% of CO2 travels in plasma as HCO3-; the reaction reverses in the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O to H2CO3, which dissociates to HCO3- and H+. Bicarbonate exits the cell (chloride shift) so ~70% of CO2 travels in plasma as HCO3-; the reaction reverses in the lungs.

questions.stem: Panel A shows a rightward-shifted dissociation curve compared with panel B. Physiologically, what does the rightward shift accomplish for the tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased total oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced dissolved CO2 content in the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased O2 affinity, which unloads more oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of hemoglobin to a higher-affinity fetal form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased O2 affinity, promoting oxygen loading in the tissues

explanation.summary: A rightward shift (raised PCO2, low pH, high temperature, high 2,3-DPG) raises P50 and lowers O2 affinity, favoring oxygen release where metabolic demand is greatest; a leftward shift does the opposite.
explanation.whyCorrect: A rightward shift (raised PCO2, low pH, high temperature, high 2,3-DPG) raises P50 and lowers O2 affinity, favoring oxygen release where metabolic demand is greatest; a leftward shift does the opposite.

questions.stem: This flowchart contrasts events at the tissues and lungs, linking the Haldane and Bohr effects. What is the net functional result these coupled effects produce at the tissues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Independent transport of O2 and CO2 with no mutual influence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased O2 affinity that traps oxygen on hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced O2 unloading paired with increased CO2 loading

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced O2 loading paired with increased CO2 unloading

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced hemoglobin affinity for both O2 and CO2 simultaneously

explanation.summary: At the tissues, low PO2 and high PCO2 lower hemoglobin's O2 affinity (Bohr) and raise its CO2 carriage (Haldane), so oxygen is released and carbon dioxide is picked up. The reverse occurs in the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the tissues, low PO2 and high PCO2 lower hemoglobin's O2 affinity (Bohr) and raise its CO2 carriage (Haldane), so oxygen is released and carbon dioxide is picked up. The reverse occurs in the lungs.

questions.stem: This figure shows oxygen molecules being taken up inside a red blood cell and a magnified view of the protein that binds them. How many O2 molecules can one fully saturated unit of this protein carry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One, at a single central site

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eight, two per subunit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four, one per heme group

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two, one per alpha chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twelve, distributed across the globin folds

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin is a tetramer of four globin chains, each with one heme iron that binds a single O2, so a fully saturated molecule carries four oxygen molecules as oxyhemoglobin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemoglobin is a tetramer of four globin chains, each with one heme iron that binds a single O2, so a fully saturated molecule carries four oxygen molecules as oxyhemoglobin.

questions.stem: This reaction sequence occurs in a red blood cell arriving at the alveolus. Why does the reaction proceed toward generating CO2 for exhalation here rather than toward bicarbonate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbonic anhydrase runs only in the CO2-forming direction

choices.label: B
choices.text: High tissue metabolic demand generates additional bicarbonate here

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low alveolar PCO2 pulls the equilibrium toward CO2 formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemoglobin actively pumps CO2 into the alveolus using ATP

choices.label: E
choices.text: The low pH of alveolar gas traps bicarbonate inside the cell

explanation.summary: As CO2 diffuses down its gradient into the low-PCO2 alveolus, the carbonic anhydrase equilibrium (HCO3- + H+ to H2CO3 to CO2 + H2O) is driven toward CO2, releasing it for exhalation.
explanation.whyCorrect: As CO2 diffuses down its gradient into the low-PCO2 alveolus, the carbonic anhydrase equilibrium (HCO3- + H+ to H2CO3 to CO2 + H2O) is driven toward CO2, releasing it for exhalation.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute pulmonary embolism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aortic dissection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lung abscess

choices.label: D

questions.stem: This handheld device with a finger probe is used at the bedside in suspected smoke-inhalation victims. Unlike a standard pulse oximeter, what does it specifically measure noninvasively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methemoglobin only, not carboxyhemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carboxyhemoglobin fraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: End-tidal carbon dioxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blood lactate concentration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arterial partial pressure of oxygen

explanation.summary: A pulse CO-oximeter uses multiple light wavelengths to distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, allowing noninvasive detection of CO poisoning. A standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeter cannot, and reads falsely normal SpO2 in CO poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pulse CO-oximeter uses multiple light wavelengths to distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, allowing noninvasive detection of CO poisoning. A standard 2-wavelength pulse oximeter cannot, and reads falsely normal SpO2 in CO poisoning.

questions.stem: In this plot of blood oxygen content versus oxygen partial pressure, the dashed curve (hemoglobin with 50% carboxyhemoglobin) plateaus at a lower total content AND is shifted so that oxygen is released less readily than the solid normal curve. Which statement best explains the danger illustrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CO increases oxygen content but right-shifts the curve, improving delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: CO only lowers dissolved oxygen without affecting hemoglobin

choices.label: C
choices.text: CO raises the P50 so tissues extract more oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: CO both lowers total O2-carrying capacity and left-shifts the dissociation curve

choices.label: E
choices.text: CO lowers content but right-shifts the curve, aiding unloading

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity, reducing available O2 binding sites (lower content) and simultaneously left-shifting the curve for the remaining sites, so oxygen is held more tightly and released poorly at tissues, causing profound hypoxia despite a 'normal' PaO2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity, reducing available O2 binding sites (lower content) and simultaneously left-shifting the curve for the remaining sites, so oxygen is held more tightly and released poorly at tissues, causing profound hypoxia despite a 'normal' PaO2.
